title: The Beria pages
summary: When Lavrenty Beria fell in 1953, subscribers to the Great Soviet Encyclopedia received a letter from the publisher with replacement pages: cut out the article on Beria with a razor blade and paste in the new pages, an expanded entry on the Bering Sea. The readers did the editing themselves, at their kitchen tables, and the book closed up as if nothing had been there. The same state retouched photographs so that purged men stepped out of pictures they had stood in. A believer's point: an edit is most complete when the owner of the book makes it.
source: Web research: Great Soviet Encyclopedia replacement pages (ibookbinding.com, executedtoday.com)
fit: The sentence: the edit as a household act. A detail the professor could have in his notebook, or James finds a copy with the stub of a cut page

title: Orwell deleted from the Kindles
summary: In July 2009 Amazon reached into its customers' Kindles overnight and deleted copies of 1984 and Animal Farm that a seller had no right to sell. People woke up to books missing from devices they owned, with a refund in their account. Amazon apologised and promised not to do it again. The point for a believer is not the rights dispute; it is that the capacity exists. A printed book needs a reissue to change; a digital one needs one quiet sync, and nobody owns a first impression any more.
source: Web research: Amazon Kindle deletions, July 2009 (NPR, Marketplace, historyofinformation.com)
fit: Why the machine still bothers with paper: James's realisation that old printed copies are the last control case. Could sit in The control case or a Frank conversation

title: The Mandela effect
summary: Coined in 2009 by Fiona Broome after many people shared a vivid memory of Nelson Mandela dying in prison in the 1980s. Since then: the Berenstein Bears that were always Berenstain, 'Luke, I am your father' that was always 'No, I am your father', the Monopoly man's monocle that never existed. Believers read it as timelines merging or the record being changed while memory stays. Psychologists call it shared false memory. It is one of the biggest threads on Reddit, and it is the exact inverse of the book: in the book the text really changed and memory is what nobody trusts.
source: Web research: Reddit r/MandelaEffect; Fiona Broome (2009)
fit: Noise that sits next to the real thing: Frank waves the 1931 edit away as 'Mandela effect for bookworms'. Good for Frank's kitchen or The gorilla mask

title: Tartaria and the mud flood
summary: An online theory that grew from about 2016: a lost world empire, Tartaria, built the grand domed buildings, star forts and world's-fair palaces of the 19th century with free energy from their spires, and a 'mud flood' buried its cities, which is why old buildings have windows below street level. History, the theory says, was rewritten and the fairs were built to be demolished. Historians point to ordinary explanations for each piece. It spreads by photographs of beautiful buildings, which is why it is so sticky: it feels like grief for a lost world.
source: Web research: Tartarian Empire (Wikipedia; The Spinoff, 2022; Explorersweb)
fit: The thermostat's best kind of chaff: it is aesthetically right and factually wrong, and it makes 'history was edited' sound mad. James can recognise his own sentence wrapped in nonsense

title: Origen and the fifth council
summary: Origen of Alexandria taught that souls existed before birth. In 543 Emperor Justinian issued an edict against him, and anathemas against Origen's teaching on the pre-existence of souls are associated with the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. Believers say this is where reincarnation was cut out of Christianity by an emperor, not a theologian. Historians argue about what the council actually voted and whether Origen taught rebirth at all. Either way it is a dated, signed decision about what Christians may believe happens after death.
source: Web research: Catholic Answers on reincarnation; Glasgow thesis 7845; Justinian's edict of 543
fit: The oldest of the deleted instructions: the soul's continuity removed by decree. A candidate interlude, Constantinople 553, or one line in the professor's notebook as edit zero

title: Don't go into the light
summary: The soul-trap theory, with whole Reddit communities devoted to it: the tunnel, the white light and the welcoming dead relatives of near-death reports are a recycling system. Something on the other side wipes your memory and sends you back, and the beings who greet you are not who they look like. The advice passed around is to refuse the light and remember. It borrows from Gnostic archons and from reincarnation, and it is surprisingly organised for a folk belief.
source: Web research: r/EscapingPrisonPlanet; r/remoteviewing 'soul traps' threads; Substack essays on NDEs and the soul trap
fit: Dangerous neighbour to the book's truth two. It is the paranoid copy of 'how to die without fear'. Use it as the version the organisation would love people to believe, and keep James's ending clear of it

title: The Gateway report's missing page
summary: In 1983 Army Lt. Col. Wayne McDonnell wrote 'Analysis and Assessment of Gateway Process' for the Army, on whether trained consciousness could leave the body, using the Monroe Institute's methods. It was declassified in 2003, without page 25. For years the CIA said it did not have the page. A journalist finally got it from the Monroe Institute's own archive: page 25 is about 'the Absolute', energy with 'no here to differentiate it from there'. The report went viral on TikTok and Reddit in 2021 and again since.
source: Web research: Vice, 'Found: page 25 of the CIA's Gateway report'; CIA reading room
fit: The page 118 rhyme: the one page missing from a released document is the one about what is on the other side. James would notice the gap before the content. Strong for The control case or Leiden

title: Six and a half thousand secret patents
summary: Under the US Invention Secrecy Act of 1951 the government can order an inventor never to publish or use their own invention. The Federation of American Scientists counts the orders each year: at the end of fiscal 2025 there were 6,543 in effect, and 102 new ones were imposed that year. The inventor is not paid unless they sue. Most orders are said to cover weapons and cryptography; nobody outside can check. For a believer, it is suppressed technology with a published annual number.
source: Web research: FAS Project on Government Secrecy, invention secrecy statistics FY05 to FY25
fit: Truth one, 'they sat on inventions', with a real figure Frank can't wave away. A good line in The money or in a Kalder speech about what continuity protects

title: Tesla's trunks
summary: Nikola Tesla died in a New York hotel room in January 1943. Within days the Office of Alien Property seized his trunks and papers, although he was a US citizen. An MIT engineer, John G. Trump, examined them and reported they were speculative and of no danger. The papers went to Belgrade years later; believers have argued ever since that the important ones never arrived. The FBI released its file on the seizure in 2016.
source: Web research: FBI Vault release (History.com, 2016); MuckRock, 2018
fit: The professor's crates in a famous version: a dead man's papers collected fast, then declared worthless. Could echo Beard Man selling the whole lot

title: The Swiss company that was the CIA
summary: Crypto AG of Zug sold encryption machines to more than 120 governments for decades. In 2020 the Washington Post and German broadcaster ZDF revealed that from 1970 the company was secretly owned by the CIA and West Germany's BND (the BND left in the early 1990s), and the machines were rigged so the two agencies could read the traffic. Most employees did not know. The intelligence services called it the coup of the century; the code name was Rubicon.
source: Web research: Crypto AG (Wikipedia); Washington Post and ZDF, Feb 2020; Schneier on Security
fit: Compartments made real: a company whose own staff built the trap without knowing. The model for the seats hidden inside a continuity contract, and for Pieter

title: Iron Mountain, the archive in the mine
summary: Beneath Boyers, Pennsylvania, a limestone mine that US Steel dug out from 1902 to 1952 is now an underground records city of more than a thousand acres, owned by Iron Mountain. The US government has stored records there since 1960, including the Office of Personnel Management's personnel files; more than a thousand people have worked down there at times. It also held the Corbis photo archive. A records company, a disaster-recovery site and a government archive in one hole in the ground.
source: Web research: Center for Land Use Interpretation, 'Iron Mountain, Boyers'
fit: The building: proof that an archive on top of a recovery site is a normal business. James can find it in a search and feel the floor move

title: Operation Legacy
summary: As Britain left its colonies it ran Operation Legacy: files that might embarrass the government were burned, dumped at sea in weighted crates, or flown home and hidden. The hidden part surfaced in 2011, when Kenyan survivors of the Mau Mau camps sued and the Foreign Office admitted to a store at Hanslope Park holding about 8,800 files from 37 former colonies. Officials had answered for decades that such files did not exist.
source: Web research: The Guardian (2012); History Workshop, 'Memory exiled'; The Elephant (2021)
fit: Records moved 'for conservation', in real life. The pattern for the review and for the professor's answer that he never published: the archive itself denies the archive

title: Maní, 1562
summary: In July 1562 the Franciscan Diego de Landa held an auto-da-fé at Maní in Yucatán and burned the Maya books he could find, writing that they contained 'nothing but superstition and lies of the devil'. Four Maya codices are generally accepted to survive today. Landa then wrote the account of Maya writing that later helped scholars decipher the glyphs. The man who burned the library left the key to reading it.
source: Web research: Biblical Archaeology Society, 'Codices'; Archaeology magazine, 'Acts of Faith'; historyofinformation.com
fit: Interlude candidate, a year after Nuremberg 1561: the book's interludes already run through printings and edits, and this one is the bonfire. Landa as the professor's dark mirror

title: Room 641A
summary: In 2006 a retired AT&T technician, Mark Klein, revealed a locked room at 611 Folsom Street in San Francisco where a splitter copied internet traffic to the NSA. He found it by reading wiring documents nobody else bothered to read. The room had a different lock and only cleared staff went in. Snowden's 2013 leaks later showed the programme's scale.
source: Web research: Mark Klein affidavit and EFF case files; NSA surveillance (Snowden, 2013)
fit: James's mirror: a technician who reads the dull documents and finds the count in the plumbing. Kalder or Noor could mention Klein as what happens to people like him

title: The hacker who saw a fleet list
summary: Between 2001 and 2002 Gary McKinnon, a Scottish systems administrator looking for UFO evidence, got into dozens of US military and NASA computers. He said he found a spreadsheet of 'non-terrestrial officers' and records of 'fleet-to-fleet transfers'. The hacking is documented; what he saw is only his word. The US fought for ten years to extradite him; the UK blocked it in 2012 on health grounds.
source: Web research: silicon.com interview (2005, via attrition.org); TechSpot
fit: A list with names and an obscure heading, found by a man who reads systems: very close to the payload. James may know the story and be frightened by it

title: The cold fusion editor
summary: Eugene Mallove, MIT science writer and editor of Infinite Energy magazine, the loudest defender of cold fusion, was beaten to death in May 2004 outside a house he owned in Connecticut. Believers immediately said he was killed for pushing suppressed energy. The courts tied it to a dispute over the house, and a man was convicted of the murder years later; he still denies it. Both readings are still argued online.
source: Web research: MIT Technology Review (2004); Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (2016); NBC Connecticut
fit: A test for 'they killed people who noticed': the real record gives an ordinary motive, and that is exactly how the review's endings are meant to look. Good for Frank, or for James doubting himself

title: The bankers who died in 2014
summary: In early 2014 a run of deaths of finance workers in London, New York and Hong Kong, several at JPMorgan, made headlines: falls from buildings, apparent suicides, within weeks of each other, during the rate-rigging investigations. Believers said they knew too much. Statisticians answered with the clustering illusion: in an industry that size, such runs happen by chance. The argument about whether a pattern means anything is the story.
source: Web research: Wall Street on Parade (2014-15); mathbabe.org, 'JP Morgan suicides and the clustering illusion'
fit: James works for a bank and reads counts for a living. The clustering argument is his own professional question turned on his colleagues. No names should be used

title: Cicada 3301
summary: In January 2012 an image appeared online: 'We are looking for highly intelligent individuals.' Solvers followed a chain through cryptography, old books, Tor sites and posters taped to poles in cities on several continents. Some who finished say they were contacted privately and asked to keep quiet. Three rounds ran until 2014. Nobody has credibly identified who was behind it.
source: Web research: Cicada 3301 coverage (2012-2014)
fit: The organisation's recruitment is inference, not telling: those who ask well are invited. Fits the MindBook point that the Housed infer the fact

title: The Distributed Idea Suppression Complex
summary: Mathematician Eric Weinstein's name for how institutions keep new ideas out without anyone coordinating: peer review, funding committees, press and polite ridicule, each doing its ordinary job, adding up to a wall. He links it to the stall in fundamental physics since the 1970s. Critics say he is explaining his own rejection. He presents it as a conspiracy with no conspirators, which is its interesting part.
source: Web research: P2P Foundation wiki, 'Distributed Idea Suppression Complex'; Nonzero, 'Is Eric Weinstein a crackpot?'
fit: A believer's vocabulary for compartments and for the millions of helpers who each have one small reason. Frank could use the phrase against James, or James for the organisation

title: The dead internet
summary: A 2021 forum post grew into a theory: most of the internet since about 2016 is bots and generated content talking to each other, and real people are a shrinking minority being steered. Then generative AI arrived and parts of it stopped sounding mad. The original theory adds a controlling hand; the evidence mostly shows commercial spam at scale.
source: Web research: 'Dead Internet Theory' (Agora Road forum, 2021; The Atlantic coverage)
fit: The board card 'Doubt is cheaper': the modern thermostat does not need lies, only noise. Kalder or the old head can say it at the dinner

title: The city under Khafre
summary: In March 2025 Italian researchers Corrado Malanga and Filippo Biondi claimed radar scans showed vertical shafts and chambers hundreds of metres below the Pyramid of Khafre: a hidden city or an energy plant. It went viral in days. Egyptologists, including Zahi Hawass, said the method cannot see that deep and the claims were not peer-reviewed. Believers took the dismissal as confirmation.
source: Web research: Egyptian Streets (26 March 2025); The Express Tribune; Decrypt
fit: A 2025 example of the gorilla standing next to the real question: a giant claim on social media makes every careful anomaly look silly. Frank can show it on his phone

title: The interstellar visitor
summary: In July 2025 astronomers found 3I/ATLAS, only the third object seen coming from outside the solar system. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb publicly asked whether it could be technology and listed anomalies; most astronomers said it is a comet. The story ran for months in podcasts and tabloids. A tenured scientist was mocked in public for raising the question, which was itself the lesson a believer took away.
source: Web research: Yahoo fact check; Interesting Engineering; Jerusalem Post; Higgypop threads
fit: The ridicule rung in the present day, for the reader's own news memory. A line in Twenty minutes or at the corporate day

title: The 2026 UFO files
summary: On 20 February 2026 President Trump ordered agencies to release UFO files. The Pentagon's PURSUE site published six batches from May to September 2026: hundreds of documents, videos and audio, from Apollo crew reports to military footage of orbs. Congress had already ordered, in the FY2026 defence law, a 300-day search for UAP records and intercept data back to 2004. Skeptics said much of it was old or blurry; the Pentagon said the cases were unresolved and the public could draw its own conclusions.
source: Web research: United States UFO files (Wikipedia); CNN (8 May 2026); CBS; NewsNation; UFOUAP.com (Feb 2026)
fit: Disclosure as the heating half of the thermostat: a flood of material, no conclusion. Places the book in the reader's present; the bar TV in the pub can be showing it

title: The New Jersey drones
summary: From November 2024, thousands of people in New Jersey and nearby states reported large lit drones over towns, reservoirs and military sites, night after night. Flights were restricted. In January 2025 the White House said they were authorised research drones, hobbyists and mistaken aircraft. Many residents did not accept it, and nothing more specific was ever published.
source: Web research: Jalopnik; Sinclair stations, 'Drone mystery persists'
fit: A real mass sighting with a boring official answer. Useful for how Ana's or Frank's ordinary world handles the inexplicable: two weeks of news, then nothing

title: The Varo edition
summary: In 1957 the US Office of Naval Research received a copy of Morris Jessup's UFO book filled with handwritten notes in what look like three different inks, apparently three people arguing in the margins about how the saucers work. The Navy had a contractor, Varo Manufacturing, retype and reprint it with the annotations, in a tiny run, reportedly 127 copies. A book annotated by several hands, reproduced by the military: one of the strangest documents in the field.
source: Web research: Philadelphia Experiment and Varo edition histories
fit: A real-world twin of the thin book in two hands. The professor would own a Varo reprint; James could find it in the crates

title: MKUltra's surviving receipts
summary: The CIA's mind-control programme MKUltra ran from 1953. In 1973 Director Richard Helms ordered its files destroyed. In 1977 about 20,000 pages turned up anyway, because they had been stored in a financial records centre: they were invoices and payment records, filed by accounts. The Senate hearings that followed were built on the receipts.
source: Web research: Senate hearing on MKUltra (1977); John Marks, The Search for the Manchurian Candidate
fit: The book's own rule in history: the money is the tell. Ties directly to the invoice and to The money

title: Four hundred journalists
summary: In 1977 Carl Bernstein reported in Rolling Stone that more than 400 American journalists had carried out tasks for the CIA over 25 years, and the Church Committee had already examined the agency's media relationships. Believers call it Operation Mockingbird and see a continuing hand behind which stories get laughed at. Historians argue about how organised it was.
source: Web research: Carl Bernstein, 'The CIA and the Media', Rolling Stone (1977); Church Committee (1975-76)
fit: The press arm of the ridicule rung, next to the Robertson Panel. Bram or the old head can treat it as old, normal history

title: The secret emergency orders
summary: Presidential Emergency Action Documents are pre-written orders for a president to sign in a catastrophe. They are known to exist, about 56 by one count, but none has ever been released, even to Congress in full. Historical descriptions suggest powers such as suspending habeas corpus or controlling communications. The plan for what happens if everything fails is itself the most secret document.
source: Web research: Brennan Center for Justice, 'Presidential Emergency Action Documents'
fit: The seats as state policy: continuity plans nobody may read. Kalder's business at national scale

title: The archive that dropped 'secret'
summary: In 2019 Pope Francis renamed the Vatican Secret Archive the Vatican Apostolic Archive, saying 'secret' only ever meant private and was being misunderstood. Shelves said to run 85 kilometres; most records closed for 75 years or more. Believers took the renaming as proof the word mattered. Scholars point out the archive has admitted researchers since 1881.
source: Web research: Vatican News (October 2019)
fit: The foundation's own politeness. Aylin's reading room can borrow the Vatican's line: we are not secret, only private

title: Missing 411
summary: Former detective David Paulides has collected cases of people vanishing in American national parks: often near boulder fields or water, often in sudden bad weather, sometimes found far away with clothes removed, and tracking dogs unable to pick up a scent. He says the cases are not counted properly and the pattern is ignored; critics say he picks cases to fit. The books and films have a large following.
source: Web research: David Paulides, Missing 411 series (from 2011)
fit: Each ending plausible, with the dogs failing: a grim echo of the review and of Buddy. Use as a whisper, not as the book's mechanism

title: Bohemian Grove
summary: Every July since the late 19th century, powerful men have gathered in a private redwood camp in California. It opens with a ceremony called the Cremation of Care, robed members burning an effigy before a giant owl statue. Members say it is theatre and a holiday. In 1971 Richard Nixon was recorded describing it; in 2000 a radio host filmed the ceremony secretly.
source: Web research: Bohemian Grove histories
fit: The long table's holiday: handlers who believe their own story need ritual. A detail Bram can let slip

title: The Denver airport
summary: Denver International Airport opened in 1995, late and far over budget. Believers point to apocalyptic murals, a dedication stone mentioning a 'New World Airport Commission', a giant blue horse statue that killed its sculptor, and rumoured tunnels that lead to a bunker for the elite. The airport now sells merchandise mocking the theories, which believers find more suspicious, not less.
source: Web research: Denver airport conspiracy coverage
fit: Seats in plain sight, made into a joke: exactly what the organisation would want the real seats confused with
